name: Discourse markers in speech
subtitle: Small words like actually, anyway, well and by the way do a job in conversation: they correct, change the topic or give you time to think. They belong to spoken English, and actually does not mean "currently".

concept.exampleHtml: You're from Leeds, aren't you? — Actually, I'm from Bradford. — By the way, have you got Olga's number? — Anyway, I'd better go.

qa.html: A discourse marker does not add facts. It tells the listener what you are doing in the conversation: correcting, changing the subject, closing a topic or buying time. Most of them start a sentence and are followed by a comma.

Actually corrects or gives surprising news: "You're from Leeds, aren't you?" "Actually, I'm from Bradford." By the way adds a new topic: By the way, have you seen Amira? Anyway closes a topic or goes back to the main point: Anyway, I'd better go.

Well gives you time before an answer, often when it is difficult or the answer is "no": Well, I'm not sure. I mean explains or repeats what you just said in a better way: It's far, I mean, about two hours by train. You know checks that the listener understands: It's a small village, you know. Right and so start a new step or a new conversation: Right, let's begin. So, how was your weekend?

Actually does not mean "currently". It means "in fact" or "really". For "at this time", say at the moment or currently. ✗ Actually I'm studying English. (if you mean "now") → ✓ I'm currently studying English.

concept.noteHtml: These words are informal and spoken. They are fine in chats, phone calls and friendly emails. In a formal essay or report, leave them out (use in fact or incidentally if you need something similar). Do not use too many in one answer: one marker for each job is enough. Some markers can move: I actually like it is also correct, and you know and I mean often come in the middle of a sentence. Compare well as a marker (Well, I don't know) with well as an adverb (She sings well). For other small words that change the focus, see Focus adverbs. For linking words in written English, see Formal linkers.

items: By the way, anyway, well, right, so: at the start, then a comma.
Actually: at the start (Actually, I'm busy) or in the middle (I actually like it).
You know, I mean: often in the middle or at the end.
Say them quickly and lightly. They are not the main message.
Actually ≠ currently. Use currently or at the moment for "now".
Spoken and informal: not for essays and reports.
One marker for one job. Too many sound nervous.

listen.note: Actually corrects what the other person thought. It is light and quick.
Anyway closes the topic. Now you can end the conversation.

listen.text: Well, I'm not sure about that.
listen.note: Well gives you a moment to think. It also softens a negative answer.

hoeren.instruction: Listen and choose the marker you hear at the start (or in the middle) of the sentence.

items.text: By the way, did you pay the bill?
Well, I'm not sure about that.
It's far, I mean, about two hours by train.

rounds.label: 1 · Correct it: Actually
rounds.instruction: You hear a question with a wrong idea and the true word. Correct it politely with "Actually".

items.prompt: Is your name Anna? – Amira
Do you work in a bank? – a school
items.answer: Actually, I work in a school.

items.prompt: Is the meeting on Monday? – Tuesday
Do you like coffee? – tea
Is Liam your brother? – cousin
Does the shop close at five? – six

rounds.label: 2 · New topic: By the way
rounds.instruction: You hear a question. Say it again and start with "By the way", as if you change the subject.

example.answer: By the way, did you see Amira?

items.prompt: Are you free on Friday?
items.answer: By the way, are you free on Friday?

items.prompt: Did you pay the bill?
items.answer: By the way, did you pay the bill?

items.prompt: Is Kwame coming tonight?
items.answer: By the way, is Kwame coming tonight?

items.prompt: Have you seen my keys?
items.answer: By the way, have you seen my keys?

items.prompt: Do you know a good dentist?
items.answer: By the way, do you know a good dentist?

items.prompt: What time is the train?
items.answer: By the way, what time is the train?

exercises.title: What is the speaker doing?
exercises.hint: Tap the sentence, then the job of the marker.

pairs.q: <u>Actually</u>, the meeting is on Tuesday, not Monday.
<u>By the way</u>, did you see Amira yesterday?
<u>Anyway</u>, I'd better go. I have a train to catch.
<u>Well</u>, I'm not sure. Let me think.
It's quite far, <u>I mean</u>, about two hours by bus.
<u>Right</u>, let's look at the next slide.

exercises.title: Choose the right marker.
exercises.hint: Read the whole mini dialogue. What does the speaker want to do: correct, change the topic, go back, explain, start, think?

items.prompt: A: You're from Leeds, aren't you? B: ___, I'm from Bradford. It's near Leeds.
items.why: B corrects A's idea. Use actually.

items.prompt: Thanks for the lift. ___, have you got Priya's new number?
items.why: The question is a new topic. Use by the way.

items.prompt: We talked about holidays for an hour. ___, back to the plan. What time is the train?
items.why: The speaker returns to the main point. Use anyway.

items.prompt: A: Is it expensive? B: ___, it depends. Which one do you mean?
items.why: B needs a moment before the answer. Use well.

items.prompt: I don't want to go. ___, it's raining and I'm tired.
items.why: The speaker explains the reason in other words. Use I mean.

items.prompt: Everyone is here. ___, let's start the meeting.
items.why: Right starts the next step. Use right.

items.prompt: Zofia is ___ studying in Leeds. She finishes in June.
items.why: It means "at this time". Actually does not mean this. Use currently.

items.prompt: It's hard to explain, ___. It's a bit like football, but with your hands.
items.why: The speaker hopes the listener understands. Use you know.

exercises.title: Actually or currently?
exercises.hint: Actually = in fact (the truth is different or surprising). Currently = at this time.

rows.term: Mei is ___ on holiday, so she can't answer. She comes back on Monday.
I thought the book was cheap, but ___ it cost £40.
Tom is ___ looking for a flat in Bristol.
She ___ speaks four languages. Nobody knew!
The shop is ___ closed for repairs. It opens again in May.
I didn't expect to like the film, but ___ it was great.

exercises.title: Marker or not?
exercises.hint: A marker is a light spoken word that shows what the speaker is doing. In the other sentences the word has its normal meaning.
exercises.hintHtml: MarkerLight spoken word: Well, ... / Right, ... / So, ... / Actually, ...Not a markerNormal meaning: sings well / turn right / therefore / know a fact.

items.prompt: Well, I'm not sure about that. (well)
items.why: Well gives the speaker time to think. It is a marker.

items.prompt: Mei sings really well. (well)
items.why: Here well means "in a good way" and describes sings. It is an adverb.

items.prompt: Right, let's start the meeting. (right)
items.why: Right opens a new step. It is a marker.

items.prompt: Turn right at the bank. (right)
items.why: Right is a direction here, not a marker.

items.prompt: So, what did you do at the weekend? (so)
items.why: So starts a new conversation topic. It is a marker.

items.prompt: I was tired, so I went to bed. (so)
items.why: So joins reason and result here. It means "therefore".

items.prompt: It's a quiet town, you know. (you know)
items.why: You know checks that the listener understands. It is a marker.

items.prompt: Do you know the way to the station? (know)
items.why: Know is the real verb in this question.

exercises.title: Gap text: Waiting for the train.
exercises.hint: Choose the marker that fits what the speaker is doing.

segments.text:
Mei: Tom, you're from Leeds, aren't you?
Tom:

, I'm from Bradford. It's about twenty minutes away.
Mei: Oh, sorry! I love Yorkshire.

, have you got Olga's number? It has nothing to do with this, but I keep forgetting to ask.
Tom: No, sorry. I forgot to ask her yesterday. We talked about so many things: her new job, her flat, her cat.

, back to our plan. What time is the train?
Mei: At ten past nine.
